drills.q: Why is epoll faster than select/poll at high fd counts? Give the actual complexity.
drills.a: select/poll re-scan the whole watched list every call (O(n)/call) regardless of what changed. epoll keeps the interest list in the kernel (rbtree via epoll_ctl) and pushes ready fds onto a separate ready-list via driver callbacks; epoll_wait just drains that list, so cost is O(1) per ready event, not per watched fd. epoll_ctl itself is O(log n).

drills.q: Explain edge-triggered vs level-triggered epoll and the bug that shows up from getting it wrong.
drills.a: LT re-fires while the fd stays ready. ET fires only on the transition to ready, so a handler that doesn't read-loop to EAGAIN never gets told about remaining buffered data again — connections silently stop receiving data with no error or crash.

drills.q: Walk through what happens, syscall by syscall, when io_uring reads a file versus epoll+read().
drills.a: epoll+read needs at least 2 syscalls (epoll_wait to learn readiness, read() for bytes) plus one-time epoll_ctl setup. io_uring separates submission (SQE written to a shared-memory ring, no syscall) from notification (io_uring_enter, one syscall that can submit/reap a whole batch), so N reads can complete in roughly 1 syscall instead of up to 2N.

drills.q: What is SQPOLL and what does it cost?
drills.a: IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL spins up a kernel thread that continuously polls the submission queue so the app never calls io_uring_enter() in steady state -- zero submission syscalls. Cost: that thread pins a full CPU core continuously polling whether or not there's work.

drills.q: Why has Google disabled io_uring by default in ChromeOS, Android, and production servers?
drills.a: io_uring's kernel-side complexity made it disproportionately exploitable -- roughly 60% of Google's kCTF bug bounty submissions target it, ~$1M paid out, including CVE-2024-0582 (use-after-free giving read/write on freed kernel pages). Google chose to disable it by default rather than accept that risk.

drills.q: What does sendfile() actually save, concretely?
drills.a: It moves data file-to-socket entirely inside the kernel (page cache to NIC), avoiding the userspace round trip that read()+write() requires. A measured 2.5GiB transfer took 2,972 syscalls with sendfile vs 131,093 with read+write, about a 44x reduction.

drills.q: When would mmap be the wrong choice for reading a large file?
drills.a: For a single sequential pass -- mmap faults pages in lazily on first touch and loses the kernel's sequential readahead that read() benefits from, so it can generate more minor page faults (~1-10us each) than a straight buffered read() loop. mmap wins for repeated random-access workloads (e.g. LMDB).

drills.q: Design the I/O model for serving 1 million idle-most-of-the-time WebSocket connections from one box.
drills.a: Thread-per-connection is disqualified by stack memory and scheduler thrash at that scale. select/poll are disqualified by O(n)-per-call cost against a million mostly-idle fds. epoll (LT is fine since traffic is bursty/idle) scales with actual activity, not watched count. io_uring is an option only if the workload becomes genuinely I/O-saturated and batching applies.

drills.q: What's the difference between splice() and sendfile()?
drills.a: sendfile() is specifically file-descriptor-to-socket (the narrower, older interface). splice() is the general primitive moving data between a pipe and any other fd (including pipe-to-pipe), which is how socket-to-socket proxying (nginx, HAProxy) stays zero-copy when neither side is a plain file.

drills.q: A colleague proposes replacing your epoll-based service with io_uring purely for the performance win. What do you check first?
drills.a: Whether the workload is actually syscall-bound (profile with strace -c/perf before assuming batching helps); the deployment's trust boundary (multi-tenant/shared-kernel exposure to io_uring's CVE history vs a trusted single-tenant service); and whether seccomp/container runtime policy already restricts io_uring (containerd's default profile does).

drills.q: Why does select() cap out at FD_SETSIZE (typically 1024), and does poll() fix the underlying scaling problem?
drills.a: FD_SETSIZE is a compile-time bitmap size baked into the ABI; raising it isn't portable and doesn't address the real cost. poll() removes the hard cap with a dynamically sized array but keeps the O(n)-per-call scan, so it still hits the same throughput wall at high fd counts with high churn, just at a higher ceiling.
